question:
I'm CTO at a 140-person logistics SaaS. Three product lines, one engineering group of about 60 in nine squads. Every sprint overflows: we plan around 40 points, ship 25, and carry the rest into the next one. Marketing wants a feature a week for the growth push and says quality is engineering's problem; engineering says the churn numbers come from bugs. My head of engineering has set a "stretch" target of 40% more throughput by Q1 and tied the squad leads' bonus to it. Most developers sit on two or three squads at once, because the CEO's rule is that nobody is idle. Last month a bad release took the customer portal down for four hours; the postmortem named the developer who merged it, and he's now on a performance plan. The CEO's answer to all of this is to buy AI coding tools so we can "do both".

I need a two-page memo for the CEO that says what's actually going on here, what to change first and why that first, and where the thinking you're drawing on disagrees with itself.

MEMORANDUM
TO: Chief Executive Officer
FROM: Chief Technology Officer
DATE: October 31, 2026
SUBJECT: Systemic Diagnosis of Product Engineering Performance, Root Causes, and Recommended Strategy
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
Our current operational bottlenecks—sprint spillover (planning 40 points, shipping 25), quality degradation, customer portal outages, and inter-departmental friction—are not caused by poor developer motivation or a lack of coding tools. They are the predictable consequences of systemic organizational anti-patterns[1][2].
Optimizing for 100% individual utilization across multiple squads, setting point-based throughput targets, and enforcing individual blame for complex system failures have created severe context-switching overhead, perverse incentives, and systemic fragility[3][4][5][6]. Buying AI coding tools into this environment will not solve the issue; accelerating code generation without fixing pipeline bottlenecks will simply push unverified work faster into an already clogged system[7][8].
Below is a detailed systemic diagnosis, a prioritized intervention roadmap, and an analysis of the theoretical trade-offs inherent in these management frameworks.
PART 1: WHAT IS ACTUALLY GOING ON HERE (SYSTEMIC DIAGNOSIS)
1. The 100% Utilization Trap & Queueing Bottlenecks
Systemic Mechanism: Developers are assigned across 2 to 3 squads simultaneously to ensure "nobody is idle."
Operational Impact: In queueing theory and operational dynamics, running a system at near 100% resource utilization causes queue lengths and wait times to approach infinity[6][9].
Organizational Design Mismatch: In Org Topologies terms, we are operating in a Resource Topology—maximizing individual resource busy-ness rather than end-to-end value flow[6][10]. Developers forced to context-switch suffer cognitive sequencing penalties, where frequent task interruptions significantly spike error rates and destroy effective focus[5][11]. Furthermore, splitting 60 engineers across 9 squads while multi-tasking inflates cross-squad communication overhead exponentially, reducing effective team output[12][13].
2. Perverse Incentives & Goodhart’s Law ("Fixes That Fail")
Systemic Mechanism: A 40% throughput stretch goal tied to squad leads' bonuses, alongside Marketing's demand for a "feature a week."
Operational Impact: Under Goodhart’s Law, when a measure (story point velocity) becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure[3][14]. Tying financial rewards to points encourages squads to inflate estimates or perform low-quality work to meet artificial deadlines[15][16].
Feedback Loop: This creates a classic "Fixes That Fail" system archetype[17]. Pushing for output forces developers into an Efficiency-Thoroughness Trade-Off (ETTO)—sacrificing testing and architecture (thoroughness) for speed (efficiency)[18]. The resulting technical debt generates production bugs, which cause customer churn and force reactive firefighting, ultimately lowering net throughput further[17][19].
[Throughput Pressure] ──(+)──> [Corner Cutting / ETTO] ──(+)──> [Defects & Technical Debt]
        ▲                                                                │
        └─────────────( - Unintended Reinforcing Loop)───────────────────┘

3. Blame Culture vs. Just Culture Failures
Systemic Mechanism: Placing the developer who merged a bad release on a performance plan following a 4-hour outage.
Operational Impact: Human error is a symptom of deeper systemic flaws, not the root cause[1][20]. Placing individual blame creates a Blame Cycle: managers assume rule compliance solves safety, employees lose trust and hide near-misses, and latent organizational weaknesses (e.g., inadequate deployment guardrails, lack of automated staging tests) remain unaddressed[4][21][22][23].
Cultural Cost: Scapegoating destroys psychological safety and reporting transparency, which are empirical prerequisites for high-performing software delivery[24][25][26].
4. The AI Tooling Fallacy
Systemic Mechanism: Buying AI coding tools to "do both" (increase feature output and maintain quality).
Operational Impact: Theory of Constraints shows that optimizing a non-bottleneck phase provides zero system-level benefit[8]. Upstream requirement churn, multi-tasking delays, and downstream deployment vulnerabilities are our primary bottlenecks. Accelerating raw code generation without fixing work-in-progress (WIP) constraints is a local optimization ("water-scrum-fall") that will flood our pipeline with untested code, aggravating outages[7][27].
PART 2: WHAT TO CHANGE FIRST (AND WHY THAT FIRST)
To recover stability and flow, we must execute interventions in strict sequence based on leverage points[2][28].
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ STEP 1: Single-Squad Allocation & Capped WIP (Stop Context-Switching)    │
└────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                     ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ STEP 2: Establish a Just Culture & Blameless Reviews (Restore Trust)    │
└────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                     ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ STEP 3: Decouple Point Targets from Compensation (Eliminate Perversity) │
└────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                     ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ STEP 4: Redirect AI Tools to Pipeline Guardrails (Fix the Bottleneck)   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Priority 1: Establish Single-Squad Allocation & Cap Work-in-Progress (WIP)
Action: Immediately eliminate multi-squad assignments. Assign each developer to exactly one dedicated squad. Set strict WIP limits at the squad level (e.g., maximum 3 active epics across the group)[29][30][31].
Why First: We cannot measure baseline velocity or stabilize delivery while developers lose 20–40% of their day to context-switching[5]. Capping WIP forces teams to "stop starting, start finishing," exposed real system dependencies, and immediately reduces cycle time[11][29].
Priority 2: Shift from Blame to a "Just Culture" Framework
Action: Remove the developer involved in the portal outage from the performance plan. Replace punitive root-cause postmortems with Blameless Postmortems / Learning Reviews[22][32]. Apply Reason’s Substitution Test during incidents: "Could a peer with similar training, under the same high-pressure circumstances, have made the same error?"[33][34][35].
Why Second: Without psychological safety, engineers will pad estimates, conceal architectural risks, and resist taking ownership[23][25]. Restoring trust is a prerequisite for accurate data and operational transparency[22][36].
Priority 3: Decouple Compensation from Velocity & Align Metrics
Action: Rescind the 40% throughput bonus target for squad leads. Replace point-velocity metrics with joint engineering-product outcomes: Mean Time to Recovery (MTTR), Change Failure Rate, and Unbroken Customer Flow Time[3][37].
Why Third: This dismantles the perverse incentive structure driving developers to choose short-term output over long-term stability[15][16][38].
Priority 4: Re-anchor AI Deployment Around Automated Quality Guardrails
Action: Rechannel AI investments away from raw code generation and into automated test generation, static code analysis, continuous integration checks, and automated regression detection[7][39].
Why Fourth: AI tools amplify existing pipeline dynamics[39]. Once WIP is capped and safety culture is established, AI guardrails protect release quality while teams deliver features at a sustainable pace[7][40].
PART 3: THEORETICAL TENSIONS & DISAGREEMENTS IN MANAGEMENT THINKING
To make an informed decision, we must recognize where foundational business, engineering, and organizational models explicitly conflict:
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ TENSION 1: Resource Utilization (Taylorism)  vs.  Flow & Slack (Queueing / Systems Dynamics)│
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ TENSION 2: Individual Accountability         vs.  Systemic Determinism (HPI / Just Culture)  │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ TENSION 3: Point Velocity & Output           vs.  Outcome Value & Goodhart's Law         │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Resource Utilization (Taylorism) vs. Flow & Slack (Queueing Theory / Systems Thinking)
The Conflict: Traditional managerial accounting (e.g., standard labor variance, scientific management) treats unassigned or idle human capacity as financial waste[41][42]. In contrast, Systems Dynamics and Lean engineering prove that knowledge work requires slack capacity; operating at 100% capacity creates exponential delays and systemic fragility[6][9][30].
Executive Takeaway: We must explicitly choose whether our engineering group is designed as a rigid manufacturing line (Resource Topology) or an agile software machine (Delivery/Adaptive Topology)[6][10].
Individual Accountability vs. Systemic Determinism (Just Culture Tensions)
The Conflict: Human Performance Improvement (HPI) shows that over 80% of errors are organizationally induced by latent workplace conditions[1][43]. However, organizational behavior literature cautions against total "no-fault" passivity, which can blur accountability for reckless or intentional non-compliance[35][44].
Executive Takeaway: A Just Culture is not a blame-free vacuum; it draws a sharp, transparent line between blameless system errors (due to poor tooling or rushing) and reckless conduct[22][44].
Output-Based Velocity vs. Value Outcomes
The Conflict: Classical project planning demands predictable output volume (points per sprint) for financial forecasting[45][46]. However, empirical software studies show that story points are arbitrary internal proxies that distort reality under executive target-setting[3][14][47].
Executive Takeaway: We must align Product and Engineering around customer value and service quality (the Service-Profit Chain) rather than feature point counts[37][48].
🎯 Suggested Next Step: Would you like me to draft a 90-day execution roadmap detailing how to restructure the 9 squads into dedicated single-product lines without disrupting current delivery?

1.chunk: It is not easy to anticipate exactly how trivial conditions can influence individual performance. Error-provoking aspects of facility*1 design, procedures, processes, and human nature exist everywhere. No matter how efficiently equipment functions; how good the training, supervision, and procedures; and how well the best worker, engineer, or manager performs his or her duties, people cannot perform better than the organization supporting them.1 Human error is caused not only by normal human fallibility, but also by incompatible management and leadership practices and organizational weaknesses in work processes and values. Therefore, defense-in-depth with respect to the human element is needed to improve the resilience of programmatic systems and to drive down human error and events.

2.chunk: Systems thinking teaches us to focus on the interactions  and influences between the parts, and to improve all the  major parts in a systemically reinforcing design that  supports a common org goal (for instance, “flow”). If each  element (e.g. policies, structures) is optimized in isolation,  the performance of the whole system may actually decline  for the desired goal (flow can get worse!). By seeing the  system as an integrated collection of interacting parts that  need to be aligned, organizations can create change that  is both holistic and sustainable.

The “blame cycle” depicted below is urged on by the belief that human error occurs because people are not properly motivated.29 In reality, no matter how motivated an individual is, active errors will continue to occur, occasionally. 6.chunk:
Resource Topology There are three common Org Topologies to know, starting  with: The Resource Topology—​a topology characterized by  frozen functional archetypes specialized in one domain. Its  purpose is to ensure that each unit is 100% utilized (i.e.  resource utilization). It is seen in “resource management”  approaches where “resource managers” (or project  managers) are responsible for planning and monitoring  resource allocation and utilization.
In this topology, the value-​creation work takes place among  the Doing Archetypes in the lower left quadrant. However,  none of these can independently produce end-​to-​end  customer value. They depend on each other due to narrow  specialization. Additionally, they lack a clear and holistic  understanding of customer value, as their work mandate  focuses solely on specific tasks or capabilities.

7.chunk:
An example of this would be development teams trying to solve speed to market issues by adopting Agile practices... only to find that the work before and after them is still using traditional waterfall methods. The result is water-scrum-fall; it doesn't solve the problem.
A second example would be an infrastructure operations team trying to solve speed to market by introducing a Kubernetes platform... but they fail to look outside of their silo to what their customers (software engineers) need from the platform rather than what the operations team think they want. The result is almost always an over-engineered solution that has taken too long to build and doesn't deliver the features the developers want; it's a 'field of dreams' approach only this time they build it but they don't come.

8.chunk: The Theory of Constraints shows us that in any process, there must be a single bottleneck that limits the total throughput of the process: in the same way that a chain has a weakest link, a process has a single slowest component. whyDo: >- Whilst it may be easy to improve some part of the process, if that component isn't the bottleneck, it will either have zero effect on the throughput because the bottleneck is upstream, or it will actually cause more pain in the system by adding pressure to the bottleneck, if the bottleneck is downstream.

11.chunk: 3. Reduce the Batch Size of your Efforts Research in the way the mind works, and countless experiences from Lean, the Theory of Constraints and Kanban confirm that to deliver value faster, with better flow and good team morale we need to focus and limit the number of things we do. Multitasking does not work. Limiting how many things you do at any given time, means reducing the batch size of whatever you are doing at a particular stage of the value chain. By doing this you will deliver value faster because you are able to focus your efforts, one of the best explanations of this fact has been given by Donald G. Reinertsen. Keeping the team focused helps them finish what they start faster. Limiting WIP is a consequence of reducing the batch size of your efforts, and not the other way around. However doing either will result in improvements in efficiency and productivity. Open Kanban does not ask you to limit WIP, but it does request that you “Reduce the Batch Size of your Efforts.” How do you reduce the batch size of your efforts? Reduce the complexity and the quantity of things you do at any stage of the value chain. In software development this would mean: reduce the number of large stories (epics) you create, and do your best to keep stories simple; also reduce the volume of stories you work on any stage of the Software Development Life Cycle; this way your team will focus, and deliver more value.

12.chunk:
A study by Buettner275 investigated large software intensive systems, and included an analysis of various staffing related issues, such as: staffing level over time (fig 14.4) and staff work patterns (fig 11.61).
If team member activities are divided into communicating and non-communication (e.g., producing code), how large can a team become before communication activities cause total team output to decline when another person is added?
Assuming that communications overhead,xi for each team member, is: t0(Dα −1), where t0 is the percentage of one person’s time spent communicating in a two-person team, D the number of people in the team and α a constant greater than zero. INVESTIGATING EVENTS TRIGGERED BY HUMAN ERROR
Overview A traditional view of events and accidents is that they are caused by shortcomings in human competence, attention, or attitude. It may be under the label of “loss of situation awareness,” procedural “violation,” or “poor” management. A new and different view is that human error is not the cause of failure, but a symptom of failure—trouble deeper inside the system. Human error is not the chief threat to system safety, but rather latent organizational conditions set the stage for error and determine the severity of the consequences. Human error is not just random. It is tied to features of people’s tools, the tasks they perform, and the operating environment in which they work. In this perspective, human error is not the conclusion but rather the starting point of investigations. The point of these investigations should be to prevent recurrence, not simply to find people to punish.

21.chunk:
Latent Organizational Weaknesses
Latent organizational weaknesses are hidden deficiencies in management control processes (for example, strategy, policies, work control, training, and resource allocation) or values (shared beliefs, attitudes, norms, and assumptions) that create work place conditions that can provoke errors (precursors) and degrade the integrity of controls (flawed controls).15 Latent organizational weaknesses include system-level weaknesses that may exist in procedure development and review, engineering design and approval, procurement and product receipt inspection, training and qualification system(s), and so on. The decisions and activities of managers and supervisors determine what is done, how well it is done, and when it is done, either contributing to the health of the system(s) or further weakening its resistance to error and events. System-level weaknesses are aggregately referred to as latent organizational weaknesses. Consequently, managers and supervisors should perform their duties with the same uneasy respect for error-prone work environments as workers. A second strategic thrust to preventing events should be the identification and elimination of latent organizational weaknesses.

27.chunk: If constraints are not managed, a bottleneck usually results, meaning that production slows and a back-up occurs at stages prior to the bottleneck. For example, in producing boxes of cereal, if the cereal is produced at a rate of 1,000 ounces per minute but the bagging machines can only bag 800 ounces per minute, this will create a bottleneck. Similarly, if on a Saturday morning before a home football game, the local grocery store has ten checkout lines but only opens four of them, long lines will result from the constraint of too few checkout lanes available. Management must decide how many scarce resources (employees, in this example) to pull from stocking the shelves to running cash registers. It may be difficult to see how bottlenecks affect profitability, and they appear to be more of a timing or throughput issue. But bottlenecks can affect profitability in a number of ways. Bottlenecks at the grocery story can result in customers leaving to store shop elsewhere or can negatively affect the reputation of the store, which can impact future sales. In the cereal example, bottlenecks in the packaging area can slow the delivery of boxes of cereal to distributors and individual stores. Poor or inconsistent delivery may drive customers to purchase from other cereal manufacturers, which would have a definite impact on profitability.

Traditional program design tools, such as logic models, help us develop, negotiate, and communicate our change efforts in a clear, linear way (i.e. Resources --> Activities --> Outputs --> Outcomes --> Impact). However, these tools can fail to account for the characteristics of complex problems, causing our best plans to fail or lead to surprising results.
System dynamics is the use of causal maps and computer simulation models to engage with this complexity and understand system behavior from a feedback perspective. Visual tools for mapping and modeling such as causal loop diagrams and stock and flow diagrams help us create simplified representations of complex systems, allowing us to identify places to intervene, test out our ideas, and anticipate their consequences. System dynamics tools help us to consider the behavior of the “whole” rather than fixating on the “parts” when addressing complex problems.

When an event is initiated by an honest error, as determined by one or more of the tools described above, the entire system that supports the performance in question should be evaluated (see “systems-thinking” in Chapter 3). Events triggered by human error are often symptomatic of a system failure. Instead of asking how the individual failed the organization, the question “how did the organization fail the individual?” would be more appropriate. In addition to the individual, what or who could have prevented the event? What flaws or oversights in work processes, policies, or procedures contributed, promoted, or allowed the error and event to occur? Because the majority of the causes of events originate in the system of controls, processes, and values established by the management team, management's first reaction to events should be to look within the organization.

One consequence of an org design with complete archetypes is that they can become independently  operating silos. Whether that’s a virtue or vice depends.
Output versus Outcome Archetypes
There is a well-​known management principle of maximizing outcomes while minimizing outputs.
Outputs—​such as number of surgeries, amount of software features, number of completed design  documents, or percentage of closed insurance claims—​are relatively straightforward leading metrics.  However, more output does not mean more outcomes. In fact, more output usually means more cost or  investment, which can lower profit (an outcome). Investing to increase outcomes (healthy people, profit) is  justified; ‘investing’ to increase output is suspect.

38.chunk: For example, suppose the manager of the used car department at an automobile dealership is responsible for the profit he makes selling used cars that were taken as trade-ins on new car sales. Some of these used cars need a few repairs to prepare them for sale. The manager has the option of getting the cars fixed using the service department at the dealership or outsourcing the repairs to another company. If the manager can get the repairs completed at a lower cost at another repair shop, and if he is evaluated and receives a bonus based on his profit, then he is likely to use the outside repair shop. Is this a good thing to do? Obviously, it is good for the manager of the used car department who will have fewer costs getting the used car ready to sell and therefore will make more of a profit from the sale of that car. Higher profits for the used car department mean a higher bonus for the manager. But what about for the dealership? Was outsourcing the repairs the right decision?

43.chunk: In 1997, Reason published Managing the Risks of Organizational Accidents. Reason maintained that to understand how organizational accidents occur requires that we look deeper into the system. Unsafe acts by individuals may trigger an event. However, latent conditions within the organization, aligned with local workplace and task factors, contribute to accidents in the form of process errors or as error-likely situations. Thus it is the combination of these latent conditions in conjunction with an active error that more correctly accounts for events. From this perspective, errors are the consequences, not the causes, of disturbances in the organization. Accidents are the result of failed controls and barriers. People are fallible, even the best make mistakes. It is human nature to err. However, events can be eliminated or controlled by changing the conditions in which people work. Managing the risks of organizational accidents requires that managers, supervisors, and staff work to eliminate latent organizational weaknesses. Reason proposes three compelling reasons why latent conditions have to be eliminated.

1.3.1 Folklore
The dearth of experimental evidence has left a vacuum that has been filled by folklore and old-wives’ tales. Examples of software folklore include claims of a 28-to-1 productivity difference between best/worst developers, and the Halstead and McCabe complexity metrics; folklore metrics are discussed in section 7.1.4.
The productivity claim, sometimes known as the Grant-Sackman study, is based on a casual reading of an easily misinterpreted table appearing in a 1968 paper1624 by these two authors. The paper summarised a study that set out to measure the extent to which the then new time-sharing approach to computer use was more productive for software development than existing batch processing systems (where jobs were typically submitted via punched cards, with programs executing (sometimes) hours later, followed by their output printed on paper). A table listed the ratio between the best subject performance using the fastest system, and the worst subject performance on the slowest system (the 28:1 ratio included programmer and systems performance differences, and if batch/time-sharing differences are separated out the maximum difference ratio is 14:1, the minimum 6:1). The actual measurement data was published727 in a low circulation journal, and was immediately followed by a strongly worded critique;1074 see fig 8.22.

The service-profit chain model, created by a group of Harvard researchers in the 1990s, establishes relationships between profitability, employee satisfaction, loyalty, and productivity. The concept is reasonably simple: happy workers make happy customers who keep coming back and tell their friends. The model itself is a little more complicated and states the following:
• Internal service quality (the support received by frontline employees from the rest of the organization) leads to employee satisfaction.
• Employee satisfaction results in employee loyalty, productivity, and the willingness to go that “extra mile” for the customer, which creates value.
• Value contributes to customer satisfaction, resulting in customer loyalty.
• Customer loyalty translates to profitability and growth for the organization.
